bullets: Clinical biochemistry and biochemical testing methods

slides.title: Lesson outline
bullets: Tests: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT); Creatinine; Fasting plasma glucose

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: Used in routine screening of liver health and to help diagnose or monitor liver problems, usually as part of a liver function panel. Some liver diseases raise ALT before symptoms appear, so the test may help detect them early.

Ordered when there are symptoms of liver damage (for example jaundice, dark urine or light-colored stool, abdominal swelling or pain, frequent itching) or a high risk of liver damage: family history of liver disease, alcohol use disorder, obesity, diabetes, medicines that can harm the liver, or hepatitis or exposure to it.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: ALT is usually measured together with AST in a liver function panel. Because ALT is found mostly in the liver, it checks more specifically for liver damage.
Physiology: ALT (alanine transaminase) is an enzyme found mainly in the liver, and its blood level is usually low. When liver cells are damaged, they release ALT into the bloodstream.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
bullets: High: Possible causes of liver damage with a high ALT: hepatitis, infection, cirrhosis, liver cancer, other liver diseases, a lack of blood flow to the liver, certain medicines (such as cholesterol or pain medicines) and poisons.

High: Cytolytic (hepatocellular) pattern: ALT and AST are raised disproportionately to alkaline phosphatase. It points to liver-cell injury; the work-up looks for viral hepatitis, fatty liver disease, alcohol, medicines and other causes.
Low: Low ALT is not common and may lead to further testing. Possible causes include vitamin B6 deficiency and chronic kidney disease.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Tell the provider about all medicines taken; some may need to be paused, but only on the provider's advice. Because ALT is usually ordered with other blood tests, fasting for several hours is often required.

Interferences: A high ALT does not always mean a condition that needs treatment. Age, sex, weight, certain medicines and dietary supplements, intense exercise and the phase of the menstrual cycle can affect the result.
Limitations: ALT is interpreted together with the other liver tests. It may help tell acute from chronic liver problems, but the ALT level does not reflect how much of the liver is damaged.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
bullets: When liver test results are abnormal, the provider compares all the measured substances to look for patterns that suggest different types of liver conditions. Liver function tests alone usually cannot diagnose a specific disease.

The liver’s synthetic function (hepatocellular failure pattern) is judged not by enzymes but by proteins the liver makes: albumin and prothrombin time (PT/INR); bilirubin also reflects the liver’s clearing work. A high ALT by itself does not mean liver failure.

slides.title: Creatinine
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Blood (serum) and/or urine  ·  Units: mg/dL, µmol/L

What it is used for: Used to check kidney health, help diagnose kidney disease, monitor known kidney problems and how treatment is working, and check for side effects of medicines that may affect the kidneys. Blood creatinine may be measured alone or within a basic (BMP) or comprehensive (CMP) metabolic panel.

eGFR calculated from blood creatinine reflects kidney health more accurately than creatinine alone. Creatinine clearance (comparing blood and urine creatinine) is less accurate than eGFR but may help in people with very high muscle mass or loss of muscle mass (age, illness, limb loss).

slides.title: Creatinine
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Urine creatinine is used to calculate the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR). Comparing blood creatinine with BUN measured in the same panel can help find the cause of a kidney problem.

NIDDK suggests that laboratories report eGFR whenever serum creatinine is measured. To reduce rounding errors in eGFR equations, creatinine is rounded to two decimal places in mg/dL or to the nearest whole number in µmol/L.

Physiology: Creatinine is a normal waste product made when muscles are used and some muscle tissue breaks down. The kidneys filter it from blood into urine; if the kidneys are not working well, creatinine can build up in blood and less may appear in urine.

slides.title: Creatinine
bullets: High: Possible kidney-related causes of high blood creatinine: kidney disease or injury (including infection, poor blood flow to the kidneys, a blockage in the urinary system or kidney failure) and conditions that affect the kidneys, such as heart failure or diabetes.

High: High creatinine does not always mean a kidney problem: dehydration, muscle disorders and injuries, muscular dystrophy, intense exercise or a diet high in meat can raise it. Certain health problems in pregnancy can also increase creatinine.

slides.title: Creatinine
bullets: Low: Low blood creatinine is uncommon. Possible causes include malnutrition, conditions that make muscles smaller (a long illness, a nerve disorder, muscle loss from aging) and serious liver disease.

slides.title: Creatinine
bullets: Pre-analytics: The person may be asked not to eat meat for 24 hours before the test, because meat can temporarily raise creatinine. If creatinine is part of a BMP or CMP, fasting for up to 12 hours may be needed.
Urine creatinine may require collecting all urine over 24 hours, because creatinine levels vary through the day. During collection the container is kept in a refrigerator or a cooler with ice.
Interferences: Certain medicines and supplements can affect the result, so everything the person takes should be reported.

slides.title: Creatinine
bullets: Limitations: Creatinine alone is not the best way to assess kidney function, because creatinine production depends on muscle mass, diet, age and activity. Its results are therefore often used in calculations or compared with other substances.

A normal creatinine does not rule out kidney disease: it may stay in the normal range in early disease and rise as the disease becomes more serious. A single high result cannot diagnose a specific condition; retesting and/or other tests are usually needed.

slides.title: Fasting plasma glucose
slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Plasma  ·  Units: mg/dL, mmol/L  ·  Population: Not pregnant
What it is used for: Screening for prediabetes and diabetes, finding the cause of symptoms of high or low glucose, and monitoring side effects of some long-term medicines that affect glucose.

slides.title: Fasting plasma glucose
slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · Reference values and decision limits · 1/2
rows: People who are not pregnant, after fasting for at least 8 hours
People who are not pregnant (WHO/IDF criteria) — WHO: 6.1–6.9 mmol/L; 2-hour glucose, if measured, < 7.8 mmol/L. The ADA/NIDDK lower limit is 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L).

slides.title: Fasting plasma glucose
slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · Reference values and decision limits · 2/2
rows: People who are not pregnant, after fasting for at least 8 hours — Diagnosis usually requires a repeat test. Pregnancy uses different criteria.

slides.title: Fasting plasma glucose
bullets: High: Prediabetes and diabetes are the most common causes. Other possible causes include an overactive thyroid gland (hyperthyroidism), pancreatic problems including pancreatitis, stress from surgery, very serious illness or trauma, adrenal gland problems and certain medicines.

Low: With diabetes: some diabetes medicines and other glucose-lowering medicines, not eating enough (especially after taking diabetes medicine) and more physical activity than usual. Without diabetes, low glucose is uncommon; possible causes include liver or kidney disease, underactive adrenal glands, some pituitary disorders, an underactive thyroid gland (hypothyroidism), malnutrition, certain medicines and alcohol use disorder.

slides.title: Fasting plasma glucose
bullets: Limitations: What a result means depends on which test was done, other test results and the medical history.

slides.title: A very muscular person who eats a lot of meat and trains intensely has blood creatinine above the laboratory interval. Which interpretation best fits the source?
options: Non-kidney factors (muscle, diet, intense exercise) may contribute; one result is not a diagnosis, so retesting or other tests such as eGFR are needed.
It points to serious liver disease.
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the source says creatinine depends on muscle and diet, and intense exercise and a meat-rich diet can raise it.

Basis: MedlinePlus: high creatinine is not always a kidney problem (dehydration, muscle factors, intense exercise, meat-rich diet); a single high result is not a diagnosis.

slides.title: Why does a creatinine within the laboratory interval not rule out kidney disease?
options: In early kidney disease creatinine may stay in the normal range and rise only as the disease becomes more serious.
Creatinine is not removed by the kidneys.
Creatinine is meaningful only in urine, not in blood.
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the source states exactly this; if kidney disease is suspected, other kidney tests are done.

Basis: MedlinePlus: blood creatinine may stay in the normal range in early kidney disease and rises as it becomes more serious.

slides.title: A patient's ALT is markedly high. What does the ALT level itself tell you about how much of the liver is damaged?
options: The higher the ALT, the larger the share of the liver that has been damaged
Nothing reliable — the ALT level is not related to the extent of damage
A high ALT confirms that cirrhosis is the cause of the damage
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the ALT level does not reflect the extent of damage; it is interpreted together with the other liver tests.

Basis: MedlinePlus: the amount of ALT in the blood isn't related to how much the liver may be damaged; ALT is compared with the other liver tests.

slides.title: Why is ALT considered a more liver-specific marker of damage than AST?
options: ALT is found mostly in the liver, while AST is also found in the heart, muscles and other tissues
ALT is not affected by medicines, exercise or age, so any change in it reflects the liver alone
ALT is released only when liver cancer is present, so a high ALT points to a tumor rather than other damage
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: AST can also rise when tissues outside the liver are damaged, whereas ALT comes mainly from the liver.

Basis: MedlinePlus: ALT is mostly found in the liver and checks more specifically for liver damage; AST is also found in the heart, muscles and other tissues.

Immunoturbidimetric and colorimetric methods of determining some proteins?
bullets: 1. Immunoturbidimetry: immune complexes of the antigen (the protein being determined) and antibody form turbidity in solution; the decrease in transmitted light is measured on a photometer; latex-enhanced variants for low concentrations (for example hs-CRP).

2. Immunonephelometry: light scattered by immune complexes is measured at an angle – more sensitive at low concentrations; for CRP, immunoglobulins, complement, apolipoproteins, transferrin, ceruloplasmin.

slides.title: Immunoturbidimetric and colorimetric methods of determining some proteins?
bullets: 3. Advantages: specific, automated, fast; limitation – with antigen excess the "prozone" (hook) effect gives a falsely low result, lipemia and turbidity interfere.

4. Colorimetric methods: total protein – the biuret reaction (peptide bonds with Cu²⁺ give a violet complex); albumin – dye binding (bromocresol green BCG, bromocresol purple BCP); BCG overestimates albumin in inflammation and hypoalbuminemia, BCP is more specific.
5. Colorimetric methods are cheap and simple but cannot determine individual proteins (CRP, IgG, etc.) – immunochemical methods are needed for that.

slides.title: Proteins. Importance, structure, physicochemical properties and function?
bullets: 1. Proteins are polymers of 20 kinds of L-amino acids linked by peptide bonds; levels of structure: primary (sequence), secondary (α-helix, β-sheet), tertiary (spatial), quaternary (subunits).

2. Physicochemical properties: amphoteric nature and isoelectric point (the basis of electrophoresis), colloidal properties, oncotic pressure, precipitation and denaturation (temperature, acids, heavy metals), absorption of UV light.

slides.title: Proteins. Importance, structure, physicochemical properties and function?
bullets: 3. Functions: catalytic (enzymes), transport (albumin, transferrin, hemoglobin), protective (immunoglobulins, complement), structural (collagen), regulatory (hormones, receptors), hemostasis (coagulation factors), oncotic pressure.
4. Fractions of plasma protein electrophoresis: albumin, α1 (α1-antitrypsin), α2 (α2-macroglobulin, haptoglobin, ceruloplasmin), β (transferrin, β-lipoprotein, complement), γ (immunoglobulins).

slides.title: Proteins. Importance, structure, physicochemical properties and function?
bullets: 5. Laboratory significance: total protein (biuret) and albumin (BCG/BCP), electrophoresis (M-spike, acute phase, nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis patterns), individual proteins by immunochemical methods.

slides.title: Acute-phase proteins?
bullets: 1. Acute-phase proteins are plasma proteins whose concentration changes in the liver under the influence of cytokines (mainly IL-6) in inflammation, infection and injury.
2. Positive reactants (increase): CRP, serum amyloid A, procalcitonin, fibrinogen, ferritin, haptoglobin, ceruloplasmin, hepcidin, α1-antitrypsin.
3. Negative reactants (decrease): albumin, prealbumin (transthyretin), transferrin, retinol-binding protein, antithrombin.

4. CRP changes quickly (rises within hours, falls quickly after the cause is removed); <3 mg/L (0.3 mg/dL) normal; very high values are more often in bacterial infection; hs-CRP – cardiovascular risk (<1, 1–3, >3 mg/L).

slides.title: Acute-phase proteins?
bullets: 5. Procalcitonin – in bacterial infection and sepsis; an aid in starting/stopping antibiotic therapy (~0.25 ng/mL in respiratory infections, ~0.5 ng/mL in sepsis; ≥80% decrease over time).
6. ESR is an indirect marker (depends on fibrinogen and immunoglobulins), changes more slowly than CRP; consider the acute-phase effect when interpreting ferritin and albumin.
